common_name: Taipei Silk Toad Lily (Violet-and-White Hybrid Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; this hybrid of Tricyrtis formosana and T. lasiocarpa is more vigorous and glossy-leaved than either parent species.

directions: Plant in moist, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, keeping the root zone from ever drying out completely. Taipei Silk is a toad lily hybrid bred from Tricyrtis formosana and T. lasiocarpa, producing branched sprays of 1.5-inch flowers in violet-pink shading to white in the throat, each tepal flecked with purple-red spotting, opening from deep purple buds on stiff upright stems clothed in glossy dark green leaves. Bloom runs later than many toad lilies, from August into October, extending fresh color into the shade garden well after most perennials have finished. Mulch with leaf litter to retain moisture and divide congested clumps every few years in early spring.

common_name: Dark Beauty Toad Lily (Alabaster-and-Purple Hybrid with Maroon Buds)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; this formosana x hirta hybrid grows notably taller than most toad lily cultivars and may benefit from light staking in open sites.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with broad, semi-clasping leaves up to 8 inches long clothing tall, sturdy stems. Dark Beauty is a formosana-hirta hybrid toad lily whose velvety maroon buds open to orchid-like, alabaster-white flowers heavily spangled with saturated purple spotting and a gold-tinged throat, a striking color contrast rare among toad lilies. It blooms later than most, from September into October, and its taller stature makes it a good back-of-border choice rather than an edging plant. Keep soil consistently moist through summer and mulch with leaf litter, dividing clumps in spring only when flowering begins to decline.

common_name: Moonlight Treasure Toad Lily (Dwarf Yellow-Flowered Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade; this compact hybrid of Tricyrtis ohsumiensis and T. nana stays far smaller than typical border toad lilies.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade, siting it where its small scale can be appreciated up close. Moonlight Treasure is a dwarf toad lily hybrid bred from the diminutive species Tricyrtis ohsumiensis and T. nana, forming a tight 10-inch clump of thick, attractively blotched leaves topped by clear yellow flowers in fall rather than the purple-spotted blooms typical of most toad lilies. Its miniature size makes it well suited to rock gardens, trough plantings, or the front edge of a shaded bed where larger toad lily cultivars would overwhelm the space. The plant goes fully dormant in winter, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the crown before spring regrowth.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Diadem blooms earlier than most mountain hydrangea cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Diadem is a compact mountain hydrangea that opens its lacecap flower heads, up to 6 inches across, earlier in the season than most serrata cultivars, framed by narrow, pointed, yellow-green leaves. Flower color shifts with soil chemistry, reading soft pink in neutral soil and shifting toward light blue where soil is acidic and aluminum is available, following the same pH-driven color response as other mountain and bigleaf hydrangeas. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and its modest size suits smaller shade gardens where full-size bigleaf hydrangea would be too large.

common_name: Angola Allegheny Spurge (Heat-Tolerant Pewter-Patterned Native Pachysandra)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Angola was selected for superior heat tolerance in the Deep South and spreads into a wide clump over several years.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, including dry shade once established. Angola is a selection of our native Allegheny spurge discovered in Louisiana, prized for heavily pewter-patterned spring foliage over an olive-green base and for notably better heat tolerance than the species, making it a dependable evergreen groundcover even in Gulf South gardens. In late winter to early spring it sends up short spikes of sweetly fragrant, bottlebrush-like white flowers at ground level, ahead of most other woodland perennials. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a broad, low mat under trees and needs little care beyond an occasional tidy-up of tattered winter foliage.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Torsa Hardy Begonia (Exotic Large-Leaf Hybrid with Red Stems)

planting.note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Torsa is a hybrid of Begonia grandis with an unidentified Bhutan species, combining large, exotic foliage with the cold hardiness typical of hardy begonia.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, dividing or replanting aerial bulbils to increase the planting. Torsa is a hardy begonia hybrid grown chiefly for its exceptionally large, rich green leaves marked beneath with a network of striking purple veining, carried on thick stems that flush scarlet-pink through summer before deepening to maroon as nights cool. Pendant clusters of pink flowers appear in late summer into fall, moderate compared to the species but secondary to the plant's bold foliage display. Like other hardy begonias it dies back to the ground after frost and regrows reliably from tubers and self-sown bulbils the following spring.

common_name: Nanjiang Silver Hardy Begonia (Silver-Spotted Spring Foliage Begonia)

planting.note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, partially shaded spot; Nanjiang Silver is somewhat less heat- and cold-tolerant than typical Begonia grandis, so give it protection from both extremes.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered site with full to partial shade, mulching for winter protection where marginally hardy. Nanjiang Silver, discovered in Sichuan, China, bears asymmetric, crinkled green leaves heavily splashed with silver spotting that is boldest on the first flush of spring growth and fades somewhat as the season progresses, with pinkish-red undersides and reddish stems adding further color. Loose, hanging sprays of pale pink flowers appear on long stems in late summer. It is a slightly less vigorous and heat-tolerant grower than straight Begonia grandis, so a cooler, more sheltered spot than full exposure suits it best.
